bodyText:
What is a Variable?

A variable is a named location in computer memory that stores a value which can change during the execution of a program. The name given to a variable is called an identifier. A variable must be declared before it is used, and the declaration normally states the name of the variable and its data type, for example: int age = 25;

Variable names in most languages are case-sensitive, cannot begin with a digit, cannot contain spaces, and cannot be a reserved keyword of the language. A constant, by contrast, is a named value that cannot be changed while the program runs.

Data Types

A data type defines the kind of values a variable can hold, the amount of memory it occupies, and the operations that can be performed on it. Data types are commonly classified into primitive types, such as integer, character, floating-point and Boolean, and derived or composite types, such as arrays, structures and strings.

An integer (int) stores whole numbers without a fractional part. A floating-point type (float or double) stores numbers with a fractional part; double normally provides greater precision than float. A character (char) stores a single character, such as a letter or symbol. A Boolean type stores only two values: true or false.

Operators

An operator is a symbol that performs an operation on one or more operands. Arithmetic operators perform calculations: addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*), division (/) and modulus (%), which gives the remainder of a division. Relational operators compare two values: equal to (==), not equal to (!=), greater than (>), less than (<), greater than or equal to (>=), and less than or equal to (<=).

Logical operators combine conditions: AND (&&), OR (||) and NOT (!). Assignment operators store a value in a variable, the simplest being (=); compound forms such as += and -= combine an operation with assignment. Increment (++) increases a value by one and decrement (--) decreases it by one. The precedence of operators decides the order in which operations are evaluated; parentheses can be used to override the default order.

Type Conversion

Type conversion is the process of changing a value from one data type to another. Implicit conversion, also called type coercion, is performed automatically by the compiler, for example when an integer is assigned to a floating-point variable. Explicit conversion, also called type casting, is performed deliberately by the programmer, for example: float x = (float) 5 / 2;
keyPoints: A variable is a named location in computer memory that stores a value which can change during program execution.
Variable names are case-sensitive in most programming languages, including C, C++ and Python.
A variable name cannot begin with a digit, cannot contain a space, and cannot be a reserved keyword.
A constant is a named value whose value cannot be changed during program execution.
A data type defines the kind of values a variable can hold and the operations that can be performed on it.
The Boolean data type stores only two values: true and false.
The modulus operator (%) returns the remainder of a division; for example, 10 % 3 is 1.
The relational operator for equality is ==, while a single = is the assignment operator.
Logical AND is written as &&, logical OR as ||, and logical NOT as ! in C and C++.
Implicit type conversion is performed automatically by the compiler, while explicit conversion is performed by the programmer through casting.
In C, a char typically occupies 1 byte of memory, although exact sizes of other types are implementation-defined.

bodyText:
What are Control Structures?

Control structures determine the order in which statements in a program are executed. Without them, statements execute one after another in sequence. The three basic control structures are sequence, selection and iteration. Selection chooses between alternative paths according to a condition, while iteration repeats a block of statements while a condition holds.

Selection: if, if-else and switch

The if statement executes a block of code only when its condition is true. The if-else statement provides an alternative block that executes when the condition is false. The else-if ladder tests several conditions in order and executes the first block whose condition is true.

The switch statement selects one of many blocks based on the value of a single variable or expression. Each option is marked by a case label, and the break statement prevents execution from falling through to the next case. The default case executes when no case value matches. Switch is generally used when one variable must be compared with several constant values.

Iteration: Loops

A loop repeats a block of statements. The for loop is used when the number of repetitions is known in advance; it combines initialization, condition and update in one statement, for example: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) . The while loop checks its condition before each repetition and is used when the number of repetitions is not known in advance. The do-while loop checks its condition after each repetition, so its body executes at least once.

The break statement exits a loop immediately, while the continue statement skips the rest of the current repetition and moves to the next one. A loop that never ends is called an infinite loop, and it is usually caused by a condition that never becomes false.

Nested Control Structures

A control structure placed inside another control structure is called nested. A loop inside another loop is a nested loop and is commonly used to process two-dimensional data, such as a table or matrix, where the outer loop handles rows and the inner loop handles columns.
keyPoints: The three basic control structures are sequence, selection and iteration.
The if statement executes a block of code only when its condition is true.
The if-else statement provides an alternative block that executes when the condition is false.
The switch statement selects one block from many alternatives based on the value of a single variable or expression.
The break statement in a switch prevents fall-through to the next case.
The default case in a switch executes when no case value matches.
The for loop is normally used when the number of repetitions is known in advance.
The while loop checks its condition before each repetition, so its body may execute zero times.
The do-while loop checks its condition after each repetition, so its body executes at least once.
The break statement exits a loop immediately, while continue skips to the next repetition of the loop.
A loop that never ends is called an infinite loop.
A loop placed inside another loop is called a nested loop.

bodyText:
What is a Function?

A function is a self-contained block of code that performs a specific task and can be called, or invoked, whenever that task is needed. Functions help to divide a large program into smaller, manageable parts, avoid repeating the same code, and make programs easier to read, test and debug. This approach is called modular programming.

Every function has three parts: declaration, definition and call. The declaration, also called the prototype, states the return type, name and parameters of the function. The definition contains the actual body of the function. The call is the statement that transfers control to the function. Values passed to a function are called arguments, and the variables that receive them inside the function are called parameters.

Return Values and Scope

A function may return a value to its caller using the return statement; the type of the returned value is called the return type. A function that returns no value has the return type void. A local variable is declared inside a function and can be used only within that function, while a global variable is declared outside all functions and can be accessed from anywhere in the program.

Recursion

Recursion occurs when a function calls itself, directly or indirectly, to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function must have a base case: a condition that stops the recursion. Without a base case, the function calls itself endlessly and causes a stack overflow, because each call is stored on the call stack until it returns.

A classic example is the factorial: factorial(n) = n * factorial(n - 1), with the base case factorial(0) = 1. Recursion is well suited to problems that can be broken into smaller identical sub-problems, such as tree traversal, but it usually uses more memory than an equivalent loop because of the repeated function calls.
keyPoints: A function is a self-contained block of code that performs a specific task and can be called whenever that task is needed.
Dividing a program into functions is called modular programming.
A function declaration is also called a prototype.
Values passed to a function are called arguments; the variables that receive them are called parameters.
A function that returns no value has the return type void.
A local variable can be used only within the function in which it is declared.
A global variable is declared outside all functions and can be accessed from anywhere in the program.
Recursion occurs when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem.
Every recursive function must have a base case, which is the condition that stops the recursion.
A recursive function without a base case causes infinite recursion and a stack overflow.
The base case of the factorial function is factorial(0) = 1.
Recursion generally uses more memory than iteration because each call is stored on the call stack.

bodyText:
What is an Array?

An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous, that is, adjacent, memory locations and accessed through a single name and an index. The index identifies the position of an element: in C, C++ and Python, array and list indexing starts at 0, so the first element is at index 0 and the last element of an array of size n is at index n - 1. Accessing an index outside this range is an out-of-bounds error.

Arrays are used to store collections such as marks of students or daily temperatures. A one-dimensional array is a single list of elements, while a two-dimensional array is arranged in rows and columns and is used for tables and matrices. Common array operations are traversal (visiting every element), insertion, deletion, searching and sorting.

What is a String?

A string is a sequence of characters, such as a name or a sentence. In C, a string is stored as an array of characters terminated by the null character, written as \0, which marks the end of the string. In C++, strings can also be handled by the string class, and in Python a string is a built-in sequence type written between single or double quotes, for example: name = 'Ali'.

Strings are immutable in Python, meaning that an existing string cannot be changed in place; an operation on a string produces a new string. Common string operations include finding the length, joining two strings (concatenation), extracting a part of a string (substring or slicing), comparing two strings, and searching for a character or word within a string.

Searching and Sorting

Two operations are frequently examined with arrays. Linear search checks elements one by one from the start and works on unsorted data. Binary search repeatedly divides a sorted array in half and is faster than linear search on large sorted data, but it requires the data to be sorted first.
keyPoints: An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations.
Array indexing starts at 0 in C, C++ and Python, so the last element of an array of size n is at index n - 1.
Accessing an index outside the valid range is an out-of-bounds error.
A one-dimensional array is a single list of elements, while a two-dimensional array is arranged in rows and columns.
In C, a string is an array of characters terminated by the null character, written as \0.
Strings are immutable in Python, meaning an existing string cannot be changed in place.
Concatenation is the operation of joining two strings together.
A substring is a part of a string; extracting one is called slicing in Python.
Linear search checks elements one by one and works on unsorted data.
Binary search repeatedly divides a sorted array in half and requires the data to be sorted first.
Binary search is faster than linear search on large sorted data.

bodyText:
C Language

C is a general-purpose, procedural programming language developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Laboratories in the early 1970s. It was created to develop the UNIX operating system. C is called a middle-level language because it combines features of high-level languages with the ability to work close to the hardware, for example through pointers. C programs are compiled, meaning the whole source code is translated into machine code before execution, which makes them fast and efficient. The standard book on C, The C Programming Language, was written by Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie.

C++ Language

C++ was developed by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Laboratories, beginning as C with Classes in 1979 and renamed C++ in 1983. C++ extends C by adding object-oriented programming features, including classes and objects, inheritance, polymorphism and encapsulation, while retaining the procedural features of C. The name C++ refers to the increment operator (++), suggesting that it is an incremented, or improved, version of C.

Python Language

Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. Its name comes from the British comedy group Monty Python, not from the snake. Python emphasises readability through simple syntax and indentation instead of braces to mark blocks of code. Python is dynamically typed, meaning that a variable's type is decided at run time and need not be declared in advance.

Python is widely used in web development, data analysis, artificial intelligence and machine learning, automation and scripting. A simple Python statement is: print('Hello, World'). The equivalent C statement is: printf('Hello, World');. Because Python is interpreted, its code is normally executed line by line rather than compiled in full beforehand, which makes development faster but execution generally slower than compiled C or C++.

Programming Paradigms

A programming paradigm is a style or approach to writing programs. Procedural programming organises code into procedures or functions, as in C. Object-oriented programming organises code around objects that combine data and the functions that operate on them, as in C++ and Python. Structured programming avoids unrestricted jumps and relies on sequence, selection and iteration.
keyPoints: C was developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Laboratories in the early 1970s.
C was created to develop the UNIX operating system.
C is called a middle-level language because it combines high-level features with low-level hardware access.
C++ was developed by Bjarne Stroustrup, beginning as C with Classes in 1979 and renamed C++ in 1983.
The name C++ comes from the increment operator (++), suggesting an improved version of C.
C++ adds object-oriented features to C, including classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism and encapsulation.
Python was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991.
Python is named after the British comedy group Monty Python, not the snake.
Python uses indentation, not braces, to mark blocks of code.
Python is dynamically typed, meaning a variable's type is decided at run time and need not be declared in advance.
Python is an interpreted language, while C and C++ are compiled languages.
The C Programming Language was written by Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie.
